Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said that despite President Bush's low approval ratings, people will soon "start to thank this president for what he's done." Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice says "there is no greater honor than to serve this country," "So we can sit here and talk about the long record, but what I would say to you is that this president has faced tougher circumstances than perhaps at any time since the end of World War II, and he has delivered policies that are going to stand the test of time," Rice said in an interview that aired on CBS' "Sunday Morning." The secretary of state brushed off reports that suggest the United States' image is suffering abroad.  She praised the administration's ability to change the conversation in the Middle East. "This isn't a popularity contest. I'm sorry, it isn't. What the administration is responsible to do is to make good choices about Americans' interests and values in the long run -- not for today's headlines, but for history's judgment," she said. "And I am quite certain that when the final chapters are written and it's clear that Saddam Hussein's Iraq is gone in favor of an Iraq that is favorable to the future of the Middle East; when the history is written of a U.S.-China relationship that is better than it's ever been; an India relationship that is deeper and better than it's ever been; a relationship with Brazil and other countries of the left of Latin America, better than it's ever been ... "When one looks at what we've been able to do in terms of changing the conversation in the Middle East about democracy and values, this administration will be judged well, and I'll wait for history's judgment and not today's headlines." Asked by CBS' Rita Braver why some former diplomats say Americans are disliked around the world, Rice said that's "just not true." "I know what U.S. policy has achieved. And so I don't know what diplomats you're talking to, but look at the record," she said. Rice said she wasn't bothered by criticism about her or the administration's polices, saying if a person in her business is not being criticized, "you're not doing something right." "I'm here to make tough choices, and this president is here to make tough choices, and we have. And yes, I -- there are some things that I would do very differently if I had it to do over again. You don't have that luxury. You have to make the choices and take the positions that you do at the time," she said. Asked about historians who say Bush is one of the worst presidents, Rice said those "aren't very good historians." "If you're making historical judgments before an administration is already out -- even out of office, and if you're trying to make historical judgments when the nature of the Middle East is still to be determined, and when one cannot yet judge the effects of decisions that this President has taken on what the Middle East will become -- I mean, for goodness' sakes, good historians are still writing books about George Washington. Good historians are certainly still writing books about Harry Truman," she said. Rice, 54, said she has enjoyed working in the Bush administration during the last eight years, first as national security adviser, then as secretary of state. "There is no greater honor than to serve this country," she said, adding that there is also no greater challenge. Rice said when the new administration takes over, she plans to return to the Hoover Institution at Stanford University and write two books -- one on foreign policy and one about her parents.

“When one looks at what we’ve been able to do in terms of changing the conversation in the Middle East about democracy and values, this administration will be judged well, and I’ll wait for history’s judgment and not today’s headlines.”

“I’m here to make tough choices, and this president is here to make tough choices, and we have. And yes, I — there are some things that I would do very differently if I had it to do over again. “There is no greater honor than to serve this country,” she said, adding that there is also no greater challenge.

(CNN) — Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said that, even though President George W. Bush’s approval numbers were low, Americans would eventually “start to thank this president for what he’s done.”

Rice, who said that “there is no greater honor than to serve this country,” defended Bush’s record during an interview broadcast on CBS’ “Sunday Morning.”

“We could spend time reviewing the full record,” Rice said, “but I would tell you that this president has dealt with circumstances that may be more difficult than any faced since World War II ended, and he has put in place policies that will endure over time.”

Rice dismissed claims that America’s reputation overseas had been damaged. She also commended the Bush administration for shifting the debate in the Middle East.

“This is not a popularity contest. I’m sorry, but it isn’t,” she said. “The administration’s duty is to make sound decisions for the long-term interests and values of the American people — not decisions aimed at today’s headlines, but ones that will be measured by history.”

Rice said she believed the administration would ultimately be viewed favorably once its full record could be assessed. She pointed to the removal of Saddam Hussein’s government in Iraq and the emergence of an Iraq she described as better suited to the Middle East’s future. She also cited what she called the strongest-ever U.S. relationships with China and India, as well as improved ties with Brazil and other left-leaning Latin American governments.

She added that the administration had helped alter the discussion in the Middle East by placing more emphasis on democracy and values. “I’ll wait for history’s judgment and not today’s headlines,” she said.

When CBS’ Rita Braver asked about former diplomats who argue that Americans are disliked worldwide, Rice rejected that view, saying it was “just not true.”

“I know what U.S. policy has accomplished,” Rice said. “I don’t know which diplomats you’re speaking with, but look at the record.”

Rice said criticism of her and of the administration’s policies did not trouble her. In her line of work, she said, if someone is not being criticized, “you’re not doing something right.”

“My job is to make difficult decisions, and this president’s job is to make difficult decisions, and we have done that,” she said. Rice acknowledged that there were some things she would handle differently if given another chance, but added that officials do not have the luxury of hindsight when making decisions. “You have to make the choices and take the positions that you do at the time,” she said.

Asked about historians who have ranked Bush among the worst presidents, Rice said such people “aren’t very good historians.”

She argued that it was premature to make historical conclusions before an administration had even left office, especially while the future of the Middle East remained uncertain and the long-term impact of Bush’s decisions there could not yet be fully understood. She noted that historians still write about George Washington and Harry Truman.

Rice, 54, said she had valued her eight years in the Bush administration, first as national security adviser and later as secretary of state. Serving the United States, she said, was the highest honor, though also one of the greatest challenges.

After the next administration takes office, Rice said she intends to go back to the Hoover Institution at Stanford University and work on two books: one about foreign policy and another about her parents.

**Rice defends Bush foreign policy legacy, says history will judge him well**

**WASHINGTON** — Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice defended President George W. Bush’s foreign policy record, saying his administration’s decisions after the September 11 attacks should be judged in the context of a dangerous and uncertain moment in American history.

Rice, who served as Bush’s national security adviser during his first term and secretary of state during his second, said the former president’s legacy is likely to improve over time despite the low approval ratings he faced as he left office.

“History has a long arc,” Rice said, arguing that Bush made difficult decisions aimed at protecting the United States and promoting democracy abroad. She said future historians would weigh not only the controversies surrounding the Iraq War and other policies, but also the administration’s broader response to terrorism and its efforts to reshape U.S. policy after 9/11.

Bush left office in January 2009 with public opinion sharply divided over his presidency. His approval ratings had fallen amid the prolonged wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, the financial crisis and criticism of his administration’s handling of Hurricane Katrina. But Rice said those numbers do not fully capture what she described as the seriousness of the challenges Bush faced.

“He was a president who understood that after September 11, the world had changed,” Rice said. “He believed the United States had to act decisively.”

Rice pointed to Bush’s counterterrorism policies and his administration’s support for democratic movements as central parts of his foreign policy legacy. She also emphasized initiatives such as the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, known as PEPFAR, which has been widely credited with saving millions of lives in Africa and elsewhere.

Critics of the Bush administration have argued that the invasion of Iraq damaged U.S. credibility, destabilized the region and diverted attention from the war in Afghanistan. The failure to find weapons of mass destruction in Iraq became one of the defining controversies of Bush’s presidency.

Rice acknowledged that the Iraq War remains a subject of intense debate but defended the administration’s intentions, saying officials acted on intelligence assessments and security concerns that were widely shared at the time.

“The decisions were hard, and the consequences were real,” she said. “But they were made in the belief that America had to confront threats before they fully materialized.”

Bush has largely avoided direct engagement in day-to-day politics since leaving the White House, though former aides and allies have continued to defend his record. Rice’s remarks reflect a broader effort among some Republicans and former administration officials to frame Bush’s presidency as one defined by resolve during crisis rather than by its declining popularity in his final years.

Presidential legacies often shift over time as new events reshape public understanding of past decisions. Rice said she believes Bush will ultimately be remembered as a leader who acted on principle during a period of fear, uncertainty and global upheaval.

“I think history will be kinder than the polls were,” she said. “And I think people will come to understand the weight of the decisions he had to make.”

**Condoleezza Rice Reflects on Bush Years, Iraq and Life After Washington in CBS Interview**

In a wide-ranging interview with Rita Braver on CBS’s *Sunday Morning*, outgoing Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice defended the Bush administration’s foreign policy record, acknowledged the damage done to America’s image abroad, and said she was ready to leave government for a quieter life in academia.

Rice, one of President George W. Bush’s closest advisers and the first Black woman to serve as secretary of state, spoke about her years at the center of the administration’s most consequential decisions, including the war in Iraq and the broader U.S. response to the September 11 attacks.

Asked about President Bush, Rice portrayed him as a leader guided by conviction rather than popularity. She suggested that Bush understood the political cost of his decisions but believed history would ultimately render a more favorable judgment than contemporary opinion polls or headlines.

On Iraq, Rice continued to defend the decision to remove Saddam Hussein, while acknowledging the heavy toll of the war and the controversy surrounding it. She emphasized the administration’s view that Iraqis deserved a chance at democracy and said the long-term outcome would have to be judged over time, not solely by the violence and setbacks that dominated the early years of the conflict.

Rice also addressed the decline in U.S. popularity abroad during the Bush years, particularly after the Iraq invasion. While conceding that America’s standing had suffered in many parts of the world, she argued that global opinion is often volatile and that the United States remained respected for its ideals, power and willingness to act. She indicated that leadership sometimes requires making unpopular decisions.

A recurring theme of the interview was history’s judgment. Rice said she believed historians, not current critics, would provide the ultimate assessment of the Bush administration. She suggested that many major presidential decisions look different with the passage of time and that the administration’s legacy should be measured by long-term results, especially in the Middle East and in the fight against terrorism.

Looking ahead, Rice said she planned to return to Stanford University, where she had been provost before joining the Bush administration. She also indicated she wanted to write, teach and resume a more private life after years in Washington. Rice did not signal immediate plans to seek elective office, instead presenting her post-administration future as one centered on scholarship, reflection and public policy from outside government.

**Rice: History Will Vindicate Bush’s Decisions**

*WASHINGTON (CNN) —* Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Monday that Americans and people around the world will one day be grateful for President Bush’s foreign policy decisions, arguing that his administration made difficult choices in a dangerous era and laid the groundwork for a more secure future.

Speaking in an interview as the Bush administration entered its final year, Rice defended the president’s record on Iraq, the broader war on terrorism and the promotion of democracy in the Middle East.

“I think generations pretty soon are going to start to thank this president for what he’s done,” Rice said. “This was a president who recognized that the world changed after September 11, and that the United States had to respond in ways that were not always popular, but were necessary.”

Rice, one of Bush’s closest advisers throughout his presidency, has been a central figure in shaping and defending the administration’s national security policy. She served as national security adviser during Bush’s first term and became secretary of state in 2005.

Her remarks come as Bush faces low approval ratings and continued criticism over the war in Iraq, which has dominated his presidency and become a major issue in the 2008 presidential campaign.

Democrats have repeatedly accused the administration of misleading the country into war and failing to plan adequately for the aftermath of the invasion. Several Republican candidates, while supporting the troop surge ordered by Bush in 2007, have also sought to distance themselves from some aspects of the administration’s record.

Rice acknowledged that the war has been costly and difficult, but she said the president’s decision to remove Saddam Hussein from power should be viewed in the context of the threats the United States believed it faced after the September 11 attacks.

“The Middle East that produced September 11 was not a Middle East that could simply be left alone,” Rice said. “The president understood that stability built on repression was not true stability.”

Administration officials have pointed to improved security in Iraq following the troop surge as evidence that Bush’s strategy is working. Violence has declined in many parts of the country, though Iraqi political reconciliation has remained uneven and U.S. troops continue to face attacks.

Rice said she believes the long-term outcome in Iraq will shape how Bush is remembered.

“When people look back, they will see that the United States stood for a different kind of Middle East — one in which people had a chance to determine their own future,” she said.

Critics rejected that assessment, saying the administration’s policies have damaged America’s standing in the world.

“History will judge this presidency, but it will also judge the human and strategic costs of the decisions that were made,” one Democratic foreign policy adviser said. “It is far too soon to declare vindication.”

Rice also defended Bush’s broader record, including efforts to combat terrorism, strengthen alliances and confront nuclear ambitions in Iran and North Korea. She said the administration had adapted its approach over time and remained committed to diplomacy.

“The president has never believed that America could retreat from the world,” Rice said. “He believed America had to lead.”

Bush has repeatedly said he is comfortable leaving the final judgment of his presidency to history. Rice echoed that view, suggesting that public opinion in the moment often fails to capture the significance of major decisions.

“Big choices are rarely popular when they are made,” she said. “But leadership is not about doing what is easy. It is about doing what you believe is right for the country.”

With less than a year left in office, Bush continues to defend the Iraq war and his post-September 11 policies as central to keeping the country safe. Whether Americans will ultimately share Rice’s confidence remains an open question — one likely to be debated long after the 2008 campaign is over.

**Rice defends Bush foreign-policy record, says Iraq and Middle East strategy will face “history’s judgment”**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*[City], [Date]*

Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice mounted a broad defense of the George W. Bush administration’s foreign-policy record, arguing that its most controversial decisions—especially the Iraq war, its democracy agenda in the Middle East and its management of U.S.-China relations—should be judged not only by immediate outcomes but by their long-term strategic context.

Rice, who served as national security adviser during Bush’s first term and secretary of state during his second, acknowledged that the administration’s record remains fiercely debated. But she rejected the view that its policies were defined solely by the failures and costs of the Iraq war.

“Today’s headlines and history’s judgment are rarely the same,” Rice said, defending the administration’s approach as one shaped by the trauma of the Sept. 11 attacks and the belief that the United States could no longer treat instability in distant regions as a secondary concern.

On Iraq, Rice reiterated the Bush administration’s longstanding argument that Saddam Hussein’s regime posed a danger in the post-9/11 security environment. She pointed to the intelligence failures over weapons of mass destruction but said the broader strategic question was how the United States should respond to hostile regimes believed to be pursuing dangerous capabilities.

During the run-up to the war, Rice had warned that the United States could not wait for conclusive proof of an Iraqi threat, saying, “We don’t want the smoking gun to be a mushroom cloud.” Critics have since cited that line as emblematic of what they call the administration’s overstatement of the Iraqi threat. Rice, however, has argued that officials were operating with the intelligence assessments available at the time and under radically changed assumptions after 9/11.

She also defended the administration’s push for political change in the Middle East, saying the old U.S. bargain with authoritarian governments had not produced lasting stability. In a 2005 speech in Cairo, Rice said, “For 60 years, my country, the United States, pursued stability at the expense of democracy in the Middle East—and we achieved neither.” She added then, “Now, we are taking a different course. We are supporting the democratic aspirations of all people.”

Rice has continued to frame that argument as central to the Bush administration’s worldview: that repression, extremism and regional stagnation were linked, and that U.S. policy could not rely indefinitely on friendly autocrats while ignoring popular demands for political rights.

Her critics counter that the democracy agenda was unevenly applied and that the Iraq invasion destabilized the region, strengthened Iran and fueled sectarian violence. Rice has acknowledged the enormous costs of the war but has maintained that the Middle East’s deeper problems predated the Bush administration and would have confronted the United States regardless.

Rice also addressed U.S.-China relations, portraying the Bush years as a period in which Washington tried to combine engagement with strategic realism. Before joining the administration, Rice wrote that “China is not a ‘status quo’ power” and warned that Beijing sought to alter Asia’s balance of power in its favor. As secretary of state, however, she also supported diplomatic engagement, economic ties and cooperation where possible.

That dual approach—competition without inevitable confrontation—has since become a familiar feature of U.S. China policy across administrations. Rice has argued that the United States must remain militarily strong, economically dynamic and allied with democratic partners in Asia while avoiding the assumption that conflict with China is unavoidable.

In defending the Bush record, Rice emphasized that foreign policy is often judged first by its most visible crises but ultimately measured over decades. She suggested that the administration’s decisions after 9/11 were made under extraordinary pressure and with the conviction that the United States had to prevent threats from gathering beyond its borders.

The legacy of those choices remains contested. To supporters, the Bush administration confronted terrorism, removed a brutal dictator, expanded counterterrorism cooperation and challenged authoritarian politics in the Middle East. To critics, it overreached militarily, damaged U.S. credibility and left behind conflicts whose consequences are still unfolding.

Rice did not deny the controversy. Instead, she argued that the final assessment is not yet settled.

“History’s judgment” of the Bush administration, she suggested, will depend not only on the immediate aftermath of Iraq or the turbulence of the Middle East, but on whether future generations conclude that the United States responded to a dangerous era with necessary resolve—or costly miscalculation.

Rice, who served first as national security adviser and later as secretary of state, said the administration governed in an era defined by the September 11 attacks and insisted that its decisions must be judged in that context.

“We had to deal with the world as it was after 9/11, not as people wished it had been,” Rice said in an interview. “History will have a longer view than today’s headlines.”

Rice acknowledged that the administration faced intense criticism over the war in Iraq, the handling of alliances, and the perception that U.S. diplomacy had become too closely tied to military power. But she rejected the idea that American standing had been permanently damaged.

“I hear people say that America’s influence is diminished,” Rice said. “I don’t accept that. Around the world, people still look to the United States for leadership — not always with agreement, but with the expectation that America matters.”

Her tenure remains one of the most consequential and controversial in modern U.S. foreign policy. As national security adviser, Rice was one of President Bush’s closest aides during the decision to invade Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks and Iraq in 2003. As secretary of state, she later became the administration’s chief diplomat, pressing for democratic reforms in the Middle East, negotiating with allies over Iran and North Korea, and attempting to revive Israeli-Palestinian peace efforts.

Critics, including some veteran diplomats and historians, have argued that the Bush administration relied too heavily on unilateral action and left its successor with damaged alliances and unresolved conflicts. Rice dismissed those judgments as premature.

“Historians will debate these years for a long time,” she said. “That is appropriate. But I would reject the notion that we did not value diplomacy. Diplomacy was central to what we did — but diplomacy has to be backed by purpose.”

Rice pointed to cooperation with European allies on Iran’s nuclear program, six-party talks involving North Korea, and improved relations with India as examples of diplomatic achievements. She also defended the administration’s freedom agenda, saying the United States was right to argue that authoritarianism and political stagnation helped fuel extremism.

“It was never going to be easy,” Rice said. “But I continue to believe that people everywhere deserve the right to live in freedom, and that the United States should stand for that.”

On Iraq, Rice acknowledged that the conflict was far more difficult than administration officials anticipated. But she argued that the troop surge and political developments in the country had changed the trajectory of the war.

“There were very hard days, and there were things that did not go as planned,” Rice said. “But Iraqis have had the chance to build something different. That matters.”

Rice’s years in Washington made her one of the most recognizable figures in the Bush administration — and one of the most scrutinized. A former Stanford University provost and Russia specialist, she entered government with a reputation as an academic expert and left as a central participant in debates over war, intelligence and America’s role in the world.

Now, Rice said, she is looking forward to returning to Stanford, where she plans to teach, write and reconnect with academic life.

“I’m going back to California, back to Stanford, back to the life of the mind,” Rice said. “I’ve missed the classroom. I’ve missed students. Universities are places where you can step back and ask the bigger questions.”

Asked whether she expected protests or criticism on campus because of her role in the Bush administration, Rice said she welcomed debate.

“That’s what universities do,” she said. “People should argue. They should challenge. I’ve never believed that public service means you won’t be criticized. If you make decisions, especially difficult decisions, criticism comes with it.”

Rice said she does not plan to disappear from public life, but she suggested she is ready for a different pace after years of crisis meetings, overseas travel and national security briefings.

“I don’t think anyone who has served at this level ever stops caring about policy,” she said. “But there is a time to serve, and there is a time to reflect.”

As the Bush administration comes to an end, Rice remains unapologetic about its broad direction, even while conceding that the final verdict will belong to history.

“We did what we believed was necessary to protect the country and to advance its values,” she said. “People will judge. That is the nature of democracy — and the nature of history.”
